content.title: About
content.content: Iced latte is a cold beverage made from espresso diluted with low‑fat milk and served over ice. The nonfat version contains less than 0.5 % fat, making it lighter while preserving the characteristic aroma and creamy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Iced latte originated in Japan in the 1980s as a summer-friendly twist on the classic latte.
Nonfat milk is obtained by centrifugally separating the cream from whole milk.
Caffeine in a cold latte remains active, but the flavor is perceived as milder due to the low temperature.
Flavor enhancers such as vanilla or caramel syrups are often used instead of sugar to keep calories low.
Serving over ice helps retain coffee aroma longer than in a hot drink.

items.title: Energizing effect
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving alertness and reducing fatigue.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Nonfat milk provides calcium and vitamin D without extra calories.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine may boost metabolic rate, aiding calorie burning.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The cold, water‑rich drink helps maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after caffeine consumption.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can increase stomach acidity, which may be problematic for gastritis or reflux sufferers.

items.title: Added sugar in syrups
items.content: Flavored syrups raise the calorie count and can affect blood sugar levels.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Nonfat milk can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the iced latte chilled, right after preparation to preserve its aroma. Optionally add natural syrup, a dash of cinnamon, or a sprinkle of cocoa powder. Alternative milks (almond, soy) can be used for flavor variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared drink in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in a sealed container. Nonfat milk should be used within 3‑5 days after opening. Discard the beverage if it develops a sour smell or off‑taste.

content.title: About
content.content: Rugelach are small baked pastries made from a yeasted dough, traditionally filled with nuts, chocolate, jam, or cheese. The dough is tender and slightly sweet, while the filling adds a rich, aromatic flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rugelach originate from Eastern European Jewish cuisine and are often served at holidays.
They are traditionally shaped into a crescent, though round versions also exist.
The classic recipe uses butter, but modern versions may incorporate vegetable fats.
Fillings can be sweet (chocolate, nuts) or savory (cheese, spinach).
Rugelach are frequently topped with sugar sprinkles or nut crumbs.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: They provide carbohydrates and a modest amount of fat, delivering quick energy.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeasted dough contains thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Nut and dried‑fruit fillings add magnesium, iron, and zinc.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Chocolate and nut fillings are high in polyphenols, which combat free radicals.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: If the filling includes dried fruit, it can help promote regular bowel movements.

items.title: Nut and gluten allergy
items.content: Fillings often contain nuts, and the dough is wheat‑based, which may trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet versions can raise blood glucose levels when consumed in excess.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Rugelach are relatively calorie‑dense due to fats and sugar, so portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rugelach can be enjoyed as a standalone dessert, served with tea or coffee, or used as a sweet snack at celebrations. They are conveniently stored in an airtight container to stay soft.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep rugelach in a dry, cool place in a sealed container for up to 5 days. For longer storage, refrigerate them, where they remain fresh for up to 2 weeks.

hamburger-on-white-bun-1-medium-patty.title: Hamburger on white bun, 1 medium patty

content.title: About
content.content: A hamburger on a white bun with one medium beef patty is a classic fast‑food item that combines a soft bun, a flavorful meat patty, fresh vegetables, and sauces. Perfect for a quick lunch or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hamburger was served in the United States in the late 19th century.
A white bun provides a neutral base that lets the patty and sauces shine.
A medium patty weighs about 100 g and contains roughly 250 kcal.
Hamburgers are often paired with fries and a drink to form a popular "combo".
Different countries add local twists: teriyaki in Japan, meat‑free patties in India.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The beef patty provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The burger supplies B12, B6, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: The white bun delivers quick‑acting carbs that are rapidly converted into energy.

items.title: Vegetable nutrients
items.content: Lettuce, tomato, and onion add fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: One hamburger can contain 500–800 kcal, which may contribute to weight gain if eaten frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Beef contains saturated fat, which in excess can raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sauces and the bun often add significant sodium, a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Ingredients may include gluten (bun), dairy (cheese, sauces), and eggs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hamburgers are typically eaten by hand, holding them with both hands. Additional toppings such as cheese, bacon, avocado, or various sauces can be added. For a neater option, cut in half and use a fork.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best consumed immediately. If needed, store in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. Reheat in an oven or skillet, and lightly toast the bun to prevent sogginess.

content.title: About
content.content: Kidney beans and white rice is a classic combination used in many world cuisines. Kidney beans provide protein and fiber, while rice supplies quick‑digesting carbohydrates, creating a balanced source of energy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kidney beans get their name from the deep red color of mature beans.
Together beans and rice form a complete protein, compensating for each other's limiting amino acids.
In Japan, a dish of beans and rice is called “mizu‑moti” and is served during traditional festivals.
Dried beans can be stored for several years, and rice can last up to five years when kept properly.

items.title: Rich plant protein source
items.content: Kidney beans contain about 8 g of protein per 100 g, making them valuable for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are important for blood formation and anemia prevention, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Energy balance
items.content: White rice is quickly absorbed, providing rapid glucose, while beans slow the release, offering a steadier energy supply.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The combination is virtually fat‑free, suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytates that can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and cooking lower their levels.

items.title: Raw toxicity
items.content: Raw kidney beans contain lectins that can cause food poisoning; always cook beans thoroughly.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: High glycemic index of rice
items.content: White rice has a high GI; for better blood‑sugar control, consider using brown rice instead.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beans and rice are often prepared as pilaf, stew, or salad. Soak beans for 8–12 hours, then boil until tender, and mix with cooked rice. Add vegetables, herbs, and a drizzle of olive oil for flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 2 years. Cooked beans and rice keep in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.

lamb-shish-kabob-with-vegetables-excludi.title: Lamb shish kabob with vegetables (no potatoes)

content.title: About
content.content: Lamb shish kabob with vegetables (no potatoes) is made from tender lamb cubes marinated in spices and a mix of fresh vegetables (bell pepper, zucchini, onion, cherry tomatoes). The pieces are threaded onto skewers and grilled over high heat until a fragrant crust forms. The dish is rich in protein, vitamins and minerals while omitting starchy potatoes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lamb is a staple in Middle Eastern and Mediterranean cuisines.
Marinades often contain yogurt, which tenderizes the meat and adds probiotics.
Vegetables grilled alongside the meat retain their juices, giving the kabob vivid color and moisture.
Quick high‑heat grilling preserves most of the nutrients in both meat and veg.
The dish is commonly served with tzatziki or a mint‑yogurt sauce.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Lamb provides complete animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function and hemoglobin formation.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Lamb contains B12, niacin and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Bell peppers and tomatoes are high in vitamin C and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Excluding potatoes makes the dish suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic or intolerant to lamb.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Lamb contains saturated fats; people with heart disease should monitor portion size.

items.title: Risk of overeating
items.content: The flavorful nature of the dish can lead to excess calorie intake.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Undercooked lamb may harbor harmful bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of about 70 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the hot kabobs directly from the grill, optionally drizzling with lemon juice, fresh herbs, or a yogurt‑based sauce. They pair well with a light green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cooked kabobs keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Reheat thoroughly before serving. Raw meat and vegetables should be stored separately and used within 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Mixed nuts NFS (item 2269) is a blend of selected nuts: almonds, hazelnuts, cashews, walnuts and peanuts, roasted to a golden crisp. The mix offers a rich, slightly sweet flavor and crunchy texture, suitable as a snack on its own or as an addition to dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix is popular in sports nutrition because of its high protein and healthy‑fat content.
Each nut retains its unique nutrients: almonds provide vitamin E, hazelnuts magnesium, cashews copper, walnuts omega‑3, and peanuts plant protein.
Roasting is performed at controlled temperatures to preserve aroma and limit fat oxidation.
NFS mix is produced without added salt or sugar, making it suitable for diet‑focused eating.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Almonds in the blend supply a high amount of vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats from hazelnuts and walnuts help maintain a healthy heart.

items.title: Source of magnesium and copper
items.content: Magnesium from almonds and copper from cashews support muscle and nerve function.

items.title: High plant‑protein content
items.content: Peanuts and cashews contribute a substantial portion of the blend’s total protein.

items.title: Supports brain function
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids from walnuts aid cognitive processes.

items.title: Tree‑nut allergy
items.content: The mix contains several types of nuts, increasing the risk of allergic reactions.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Nuts are calorie‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Whole nuts can pose a choking risk for young children; consider offering finely chopped versions.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Some nuts (e.g., almonds) contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney‑stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mixed nuts NFS can be enjoyed as a snack, added to muesli, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or used as a topping for dishes. For extra aroma, lightly toast the nuts in a pan before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the mix in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation. Discard any nuts that develop a rancid or off smell.

content.title: About
content.content: German‑style potato salad is a traditional dish made from boiled potatoes, pickles, onions, hard‑boiled eggs and a dressing of vegetable oil, vinegar and mustard. It is served cold and often accompanied by sausage or ham.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Germany has many regional variations of potato salad, each with its own spice blend and dressing style.
The classic German version usually does not contain mayonnaise, unlike many other countries.
The salad is often prepared ahead of time because the flavors meld after several hours of resting.
Some regions add apple cider vinegar, giving the dish a subtle fruity note.
German potato salad is commonly served alongside grilled meats, sausages and sauerkraut.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Potatoes provide slowly digestible carbohydrates that supply steady energy and help maintain blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with modest amounts of vegetable oil, the salad remains low in saturated fats.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Provides fiber that aids normal digestion.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to eggs, mustard or certain types of sausage used in the salad.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The salt added to the pickling brine can be excessive for people with hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial growth
items.content: If left at room temperature for more than 2 hours, the salad can become a breeding ground for bacteria.

items.title: Vinegar acidity
items.content: Large amounts of vinegar may irritate the stomach of those with gastritis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad as a side dish or a standalone meal alongside meat, sausage, fish or sauerkraut. It can be eaten with a spoon or fork, and also used as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Before serving, allow it to reach room temperature so the flavors fully develop.

content.title: About
content.content: Walnut oil is obtained by cold‑pressing the nuts of the walnut tree (Juglans regia). It has a rich nutty aroma, golden‑yellow colour and a smooth texture. The oil is widely used in cooking, cosmetics and as a dietary supplement.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Walnut oil is high in polyunsaturated fatty acids, especially the omega‑3 alpha‑linolenic acid.
Traditional medicine has used it to improve skin and hair health.
Walnut trees can reach up to 30 m in height and live more than 200 years.
The oil is a common ingredient in vinaigrettes, marinades and salad dressings.
When stored in a dark cool place, it retains its quality for up to 2 years.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids support heart health, improve vascular function and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Contains vitamin E and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Skin support
items.content: Linoleic acid helps moisturise and restore the skin barrier.

items.title: Cholesterol balance
items.content: Polyunsaturated fats may help lower LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Brain function
items.content: Omega‑3 and vitamin E contribute to cognitive health and may slow age‑related decline.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: People allergic to walnuts can react to even small amounts of the oil.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The oil is very calorie‑dense (about 900 kcal per 100 g), so portion control is important.

items.title: Oxidation if stored improperly
items.content: Exposure to light, heat and air can cause the oil to become rancid and unsafe to eat.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Large doses of omega‑3 may enhance the effect of anticoagulants; consult a doctor if you take such medication.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use walnut oil in cold dishes: salad dressings, sauces, dips. It can also be added to smoothies, yogurts and oatmeal. For low‑heat cooking (up to 180 °C) the oil retains its beneficial properties, but high‑heat frying may degrade its flavor and nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the oil in a tightly sealed dark bottle, preferably glass, in the refrigerator or a cool dark pantry. Discard it if it develops a bitter smell or changes colour.
